name: CCHD

question.stem: A term newborn female, born via uncomplicated vaginal delivery at 39 weeks' gestation to a mother with an unremarkable prenatal course, is 26 hours old and ready for discharge. As part of routine care, the nursery nurse performs the mandated Critical Congenital Heart Disease (CCHD) screen using pulse oximetry. Pulse oximetry in the right hand (preductal) is 100%, and left foot (postductal) is measured to be 96%. The infant is asymptomatic, feeding well, and has a normal physical exam with no murmur, normal femoral pulses, and normal work of breathing.
question.prompt: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassure the family that this is a normal screen and proceed with routine discharge
Repeat the pulse oximetry screen in one hour
Proceed with discharge ensuring close follow-up within 48-hours.
Obtain a stat pediatric cardiology consult and initiate prostaglandin E1 infusion
Obtain a chest X-ray and EKG before making a disposition decision

explanation.text: The standard CCHD screening algorithm (endorsed by the AAP/AHA, performed after 24 hours of life or as late as possible prior to discharge) evaluates both the absolute oxygen saturation values and the difference between preductal (right hand) and postductal (either foot) saturations:

rows: Either extremity ≥95%, AND difference between right hand and foot ≤3%
Either extremity 90–94%, OR a difference of ≥4% between right hand and foot
Any extremity <90% (on any single measurement), OR 90–94% persisting through 3 tests, OR difference ≥4% persisting through 3 tests

explanation.text: In this infant, both individual saturations look reassuring (100% and 96%, both ≥95%), which is a common distractor leading test-takers to select "pass." However, the absolute difference between the two measurements is 4% (100% − 96%), which exceeds the ≤3% threshold required for a pass, regardless of how high the individual numbers are. This places the infant in the "retest" category rather than a passing screen.

Per protocol, this requires repeating the screen in one hour, for up to a total of three attempts. If the repeat screen normalizes (difference ≤3%, saturations ≥95%), the infant passes and can be discharged routinely. If the discordance or low saturations persist through three tests, the infant fails the screen and requires further workup (echocardiography, cardiology consultation).

content.text: Incorrect — while it's tempting to reassure the family given the high absolute numbers, this technically does not meet passing criteria due to the ≥4% differential; premature reassurance/discharge risks missing a duct-dependent lesion (e.g., coarctation of the aorta) that has not yet declared itself hemodynamically.

Emergent echocardiography is not indicated until the infant fails the full retest algorithm — jumping straight to echo skips the appropriate stepwise protocol (though echo remains the definitive diagnostic test once the screen fails).

Empiric PGE1 and stat cardiology consultation would be appropriate for a hemodynamically unstable infant or one with a failed screen and high clinical suspicion for a duct-dependent lesion — not for an asymptomatic infant on a single indeterminate screen.
CXR/EKG are not part of the standardized CCHD screening algorithm and are not the appropriate next step; the protocol specifically dictates pulse oximetry retesting first.

bottomLine: A CCHD screen only passes when saturations are ≥95% in either extremity and the right hand–foot differential is ≤3%. A 4% differential — even with reassuringly high individual values — mandates a repeat screen in one hour, not automatic reassurance or discharge.
